scientific.summary: Orion is a prominent equatorial constellation recognized by the IAU and crossed by the celestial equator.
scientific.approximatePosition: Centered roughly near right ascension 5h and declination +5 degrees; values are constellation-level approximations, not object coordinates.
scientific.relativeSizeNote: Among the larger modern constellations; exact ranking should follow IAU boundary area references.
scientific.astronomicalImportance: Orion is useful for teaching stellar evolution, recognizable asterisms, nebulae, and winter-sky navigation.
scientific.starFormationContext: The Orion Molecular Cloud complex contains active star-forming regions including the Orion Nebula.
scientific.distanceCautions: The constellation is a line-of-sight pattern; stars and nebulae in Orion are at very different distances.

observation.northernHemisphere: Generally prominent on winter evenings and visible from many northern locations.
observation.southernHemisphere: Also visible from much of the southern hemisphere, with orientation differing by latitude.
observation.seasonalVisibility: Best evening visibility is approximately December through March, depending on latitude and observing time.
observation.nakedEyeRecognition: Look for three nearly straight Belt stars with bright Betelgeuse and Rigel framing the figure.
observation.orionBeltIdentification: Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka form Orion's Belt.
observation.urbanGuidance: The Belt and the brightest corner stars are often visible from light-polluted skies.
observation.darkSkyGuidance: Dark skies reveal the Sword region and fainter surrounding stars more clearly.
observation.binocularGuidance: Binoculars can show the Sword region and a brighter patch around M42.
observation.telescopeGuidance: Small telescopes can reveal structure in the Orion Nebula under suitable conditions.
observation.locationDependentWarning: Exact rise, set, altitude, and local horizon visibility depend on location, date, time, weather, and horizon obstructions.

greek.summary: Often associated with the hunter Orion in Greek myth.

roman.summary: Roman retellings inherit and adapt the Greco-Roman hunter tradition.

indianHindu.summary: Indian sky traditions may connect parts of Orion with figures such as Mriga and other interpretations, but these are not a one-to-one scientific equivalence with the IAU constellation.
indianHindu.rashiNote: Orion is not a Rashi; Rashi is a zodiacal sign framework.
indianHindu.nakshatraNote: Some stars or regions near Orion are discussed in relation to Nakshatra traditions, but mappings vary by source and tradition.
indianHindu.uncertaintyNote: Use cautious language and avoid claiming a single pan-Indian equivalence.

chinese.summary: Chinese astronomy groups Orion's bright stars in different traditional asterisms rather than the modern IAU constellation boundary.

arabic.summary: Arabic star lore preserves names and interpretations for several Orion stars; individual names may have separate histories.

other.summary: Many cultures independently recognized Orion's bright pattern; describe each tradition separately.

astrologyRelationships.westernZodiacNotes: Orion is not one of the twelve Western zodiac constellations.
astrologyRelationships.indianRashiNotes: Orion is not itself a Rashi; any links are cultural or historical interpretation.
astrologyRelationships.nakshatraNotes: Nakshatra relationships should be presented as tradition-specific and not as IAU constellation equivalence.
astrologyRelationships.disclaimer: Astrology relationships are cultural or historical beliefs, not scientific causation.

history.ancientRecognition: Orion's bright pattern has been recognized since antiquity across multiple cultures.
history.historicalCataloguing: It is one of the modern IAU constellations with official boundaries.
history.navigationSeasonalImportance: Its Belt and bright stars are useful seasonal signposts.
history.modernInterpretation: Modern astronomy treats Orion as a sky region containing stars, nebulae, and molecular-cloud structures at varied distances.

interestingFacts.text: Three bright stars in a short row make Orion one of the easiest constellations to identify.
The Orion Nebula is a nearby stellar nursery visible in Orion's Sword.
Orion looks like one figure from Earth, but its stars are not physically grouped at one distance.

astrophotography.wideFieldSuitability: Excellent for wide-field winter compositions including the Belt, Sword, and bright corner stars.
astrophotography.beltAndSwordFraming: Frame the Belt diagonally with the Sword hanging nearby for a recognizable composition.
astrophotography.orionNebulaFraming: M42 can be framed as a standalone nebula target with a telephoto lens or telescope.
astrophotography.seasonalPlanning: Plan sessions when Orion is high enough above local haze and obstructions.
astrophotography.lightPollution: Bright stars survive urban skies; nebula detail improves greatly under darker skies or with suitable filters.
astrophotography.exposureCaution: No universal exposure setting applies; exposure depends on lens, tracker, sky brightness, and camera.

en.summary: Orion is a bright, easy-to-find constellation with famous Belt stars and the Orion Nebula.
hookIdeas: Find three stars in a row and you have found Orion.
Orion is a sky landmark and a star-birth classroom.
keyMessages: Mythology and science should be separated.
Exact viewing depends on your location and time.

hi.summary: ओरायन एक चमकीला और आसानी से पहचाना जाने वाला तारामंडल है, जिसमें बेल्ट के तीन तारे और ओरायन नीहारिका शामिल हैं।
hookIdeas: तीन चमकीले तारों की सीधी कतार देखें — यही ओरायन की पहचान है।
ओरायन मिथक भी है और आधुनिक खगोल-विज्ञान की प्रयोगशाला भी।
keyMessages: ओरायन पश्चिमी राशि चक्र का तारामंडल नहीं है।
पौराणिक कथा और विज्ञान को अलग रखें।
सटीक दृश्यता स्थान और समय पर निर्भर करती है।

editorialSafety.sourceConflicts: Cultural mappings vary; use tradition-specific wording.
editorialSafety.aiAssistedEditorialText: Derived editorial summaries must be backed by listed authoritative sources.
